questions.stem:
A 2 kg mass is being pulled up a slope by a string of tension 10 Newtons. The slope is at an angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal and the coefficient of friction is 0.3. As well as friction, the forces of gravity \(g\) and the normal are also acting.

Copy the diagram.

By resolving forces with components along and perpendicular to the slope, find the net force \(F_{net}\) in Newtons up the slope.

questions.hint: Friction = μN with N = mg cos θ; along the slope: T − friction − mg sin θ.

steps.explain: Draw all the forces on the mass: tension \(T=10\) up the slope, friction \(F\) down the slope (it opposes the motion), weight \(mg=2g\) straight down, and the normal \(N\) perpendicular to the slope.

steps.explain: Resolve the weight into components: \(mg\sin\theta\) down the slope and \(mg\cos\theta\) into the slope.
Perpendicular to the slope there is no motion, so the forces balance.
Common slips: swapping \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) in the components, or using \(N=mg\) instead of \(mg\cos\theta\).

keyPoints.text: resolving forces with components along and perpendicular to the slope
keyPoints.note: Perpendicular: N = mg cos θ. Along: F_net = T − μN − mg sin θ.

questions.stem: The velocity of a particle at \(x=-3\) with simple harmonic motion described by \(\ddot{x}=-12(x+3)\) where the amplitude is 4, is:
questions.hint: Find the centre and n² from ẍ = −n²(x − c), then use v² = n²(a² − (x − c)²).

steps.explain: Compare with \(\ddot x=-n^2(x-c)\): the centre of motion is \(c=-3\) and \(n^2=12\).
At \(x=-3\) the particle is at the centre (where speed is greatest), and the amplitude is \(a=4\).
Both signs are possible because the particle passes through the centre in both directions. (0 would be the velocity at an end point \(x=-3\pm4\).)

keyPoints.note: Centre x = −3 and n² = 12. At the centre v² = n²a².

questions.stem:
The Covid-19 1.5 metre rule is based on the premise that a person emits droplets from a height 1.8 m above ground at an angle \(\theta\) from the horizontal so that the maximum range on the ground is 1.5 metres. Show that the maximum speed \(V\) m/s of the droplets launched is given by

\(V=\sqrt{\frac{15g}{22}}\).  (Assume there is no air resistance.)

[Hint: you can assume which angle gives the maximum range…..]
questions.hint: Use θ = 45°, write x(t) and y(t) from height 1.8, then put x = 1.5, y = 0.

steps.explain: Set up axes with the origin on the ground directly below the mouth. Using the hint, take the angle for maximum range, \(\theta=45^\circ\).
Integrate with the initial conditions \(\dot x=V\cos\theta\), \(\dot y=V\sin\theta\), \(x=0\), \(y=1.8\) at \(t=0\).
The droplet lands at \(x=1.5\), \(y=0\). Find the time from \(x\).

questions.answer: Take θ = 45° (maximum range). With the origin on the ground below the mouth: \(x=Vt\cos\theta=\frac{Vt}{\sqrt2}\), \(y=1.8+Vt\sin\theta-\frac{gt^2}{2}=1.8+\frac{Vt}{\sqrt2}-\frac{gt^2}{2}\). The droplet lands at x = 1.5, y = 0: \(t=\frac{1.5\sqrt2}{V}\), so \(0=1.8+1.5-\frac{g}{2}\cdot\frac{4.5}{V^2}\), i.e. \(3.3=\frac{2.25g}{V^2}\), \(V^2=\frac{2.25g}{3.3}=\frac{15g}{22}\), so \(V=\sqrt{\frac{15g}{22}}\).

keyPoints.text: from a height 1.8 m above ground
keyPoints.note: Start y at 1.8 (not 0). Use θ = 45° and the landing point x = 1.5, y = 0.

questions.stem: A driver claims the average speed over two parts is the arithmetic mean of the two average speeds. Which case is NOT a counterexample?
questions.hint: For each case, compare total distance divided by total time with the mean of the two speeds.

steps.explain: Compute the proposed mean for option B.

steps.work: Total distance \(=200\) km; total time \(=120/60+80/40=4\) h, so average \(=200/4=50\) km/h.

steps.explain: Conclude this case agrees with the claim.
steps.work: Option B is not a counterexample.

options: 100 km at 20 km/h, then 100 km at 40 km/h
120 km at 60 km/h, then 80 km at 40 km/h
1 hour at 100 km/h, then 2 hours at 50 km/h
60 km in 2 hours, then 40 km in 3 hours
